title: Implementation of Code of Good Practice for Milk Producers in the dairy industry

lessons.title: What the Code of Good Practice asks of a dairy
lessons.html:
Why a code of good practice?

Milk is a food that goes straight from the cow to people's tables, often to children. Buyers, processors and consumers want proof that it was produced safely, from healthy cows, by people who are treated fairly and without harming the environment. A code of good practice for milk producers brings these expectations together into one set of practical standards that a dairy can follow and be audited against. Your milk buyer and the industry compliance bodies (such as the Dairy Standard Agency) use these standards when they inspect farms.

The main areas of the code

  • Milk safety and quality – clean milking, correct cooling, no residues of antibiotics or chemicals, low bacterial and somatic cell counts.
  • Animal health – a herd health plan with your vet, correct use and recording of medicines, control of mastitis and diseases.
  • Animal welfare – feed, water, shelter, calm handling and humane treatment of sick and injured animals, in line with the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.
  • Hygiene of the parlour and equipment – cleaning routines, clean water and pest control.
  • Environment – managing effluent, manure and chemicals so that rivers, boreholes and soil are not polluted.
  • People – trained staff, safe work and fair labour practice.
  • Records – proof that all of the above is really happening.

Your role as supervisor

The farm manager signs off the policy, but the code is won or lost in the parlour, the calf shed and the camps every day. As supervisor you must:

  1. Know what each standard requires on your farm.
  2. Explain it to milkers and herd workers in simple words and show them how.
  3. Check that tasks are done the right way, every milking.
  4. Keep the records up to date and report problems quickly.

A practical example: a milker in a 20-point herringbone parlour skips fore-stripping because the queue is long. Over a few weeks clinical mastitis cases are missed, milk with clots goes into the bulk tank and the buyer rejects a load. Applying the code means you notice the shortcut early, coach the milker and record the corrective action.

lessons.title: Applying the code in the parlour and with medicines
lessons.html:
Clean, safe milking every time

Most failures in milk quality start at milking. Use the farm's written milking routine and check it is followed:

  1. Milkers wear clean clothes and gloves and wash hands before milking.
  2. Fore-strip each quarter to look for clots or watery milk (signs of mastitis).
  3. Pre-dip or clean the teats and dry them with a single-use paper towel or clean cloth for each cow.
  4. Attach the cluster quickly and correctly; avoid air leaks.
  5. Remove the cluster when milking is done – do not over-milk.
  6. Post-dip every teat straight after milking.

Cooling and the bulk tank

Bacteria grow fast in warm milk. Check that the milk cools to the temperature your buyer requires within the required time, and that the tank thermometer and chart work. Record tank temperature at each collection. If the cooler breaks down, inform the manager and the buyer immediately rather than hoping the milk will pass.

Cleaning the plant

Follow the cleaning programme for the milking machine and tank: rinse, hot detergent wash, acid wash and rinse as the chemical supplier specifies. Check water temperature and chemical strength. Store dairy chemicals in a locked, labelled store away from feed, and make sure workers wear the protective gear shown on the label.

Medicines and residues

Antibiotic residues in milk are one of the most serious failures. The rules are simple:

  • Only treat cows on the vet's instruction or the herd health plan.
  • Mark every treated cow clearly (leg bands or tail paint) and write her in the treatment register.
  • Milk treated cows last or into a separate bucket, and never let that milk go into the bulk tank.
  • Keep withholding milk for the full withdrawal period on the product label or as your vet says. Do not guess.
  • Test milk with a residue test before returning the cow to the tank when the farm requires it.

If antibiotic milk does get into the tank, stop, tell the manager at once and do not allow collection until the buyer has been informed. Hiding it can contaminate a whole tanker and damage the farm's reputation.

lessons.title: Welfare, environment, records and audits
lessons.html:
Animal welfare in daily work

Cows that are calm and comfortable give more milk. Make sure there is always clean water and enough feed, that walkways are not slippery or full of stones, and that cows are moved quietly without sticks, shouting or dogs. Sick, lame or injured cows must be reported and treated quickly. Calves must get colostrum early and be housed in clean, dry pens. Never leave a suffering animal untreated – call the manager or vet.

Protecting the environment

Parlour washwater and manure carry nutrients and bacteria. The code expects you to keep effluent in dams or systems designed for it, to stop overflows into rivers and boreholes, and to spread slurry on lands at sensible rates. Water use from rivers and boreholes falls under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, so the farm must manage it responsibly. Empty chemical containers must be rinsed and disposed of as the label instructs, not thrown into the veld.

Records that prove compliance

RecordWhat it shows
Treatment registerWhich cow, which medicine, date and withdrawal end date
Bulk tank temperaturesMilk was cooled correctly
Cleaning logPlant was cleaned after every milking
Milk test resultsBacterial and somatic cell counts over time
Training recordsStaff know the routines

Fill in records at the time the work is done, not at the end of the month. An auditor can quickly tell when records were written in one sitting.

Audits and corrective action

When an auditor or buyer finds a gap, the farm must write down the problem, the cause, what will be done, by whom and by when. As supervisor you carry out many of these actions and check that they worked, for example retraining milkers after a high cell count result.

Key points

  • The code covers milk safety, animal health and welfare, hygiene, environment, people and records.
  • Follow the written milking routine and cool milk correctly every time.
  • Treated cows must be marked and their milk kept out of the tank for the full withdrawal period.
  • Manage effluent and chemicals so that water and soil are not polluted.
  • Records must be filled in at the time of the work and gaps fixed with corrective action.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a code of good practice for milk producers?

options.text: To give a set of practical standards a dairy can follow and be audited against
To decide how many cows a farm may keep
To set the price the buyer pays per litre
To replace the need for a vet on the farm

quiz.question: Why does a milker fore-strip each quarter before milking?

options.text: To measure milk yield
To make the cow let down milk faster without dipping
To clean the teat end
To check for clots or watery milk that show mastitis

quiz.question: What must happen to milk from a cow treated with antibiotics?

options.text: It may go into the tank if the cow looks healthy
It may go into the tank after one milking
It can be mixed with plenty of clean milk to dilute it
It must be kept out of the bulk tank for the full withdrawal period on the label or as the vet says

quiz.question: The bulk tank cooler breaks down. What should the supervisor do?

options.text: Add ice and say nothing
Pour the milk into the effluent dam without telling anyone
Inform the manager and the buyer immediately
Wait to see if the milk passes the test

quiz.question: When should records such as the cleaning log be filled in?

options.text: At the end of each month
Only when something goes wrong
At the time the work is done
Only before an audit

quiz.question: Parlour washwater and manure can pollute rivers and boreholes if not managed.

options.text: True
False

quiz.question: It is acceptable to move cows quickly with dogs and sticks if milking is running late.

options.text: True
False

quiz.question: Which of these are main areas covered by a code of good practice for milk producers? (select all that apply)

options.text: Milk safety and quality
Setting the retail price of milk
Animal welfare
Choosing the farm’s bank
Environmental management
